A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same SFM research work. All 21 pages of v1 and 28 pages of v2, including equations, figures, tables and appendices, support comparison. Relocated material can be matched across versions.

before.justification: Section 5 reports original experiments on ten DMControl tasks, including baseline comparisons, TD3 optimizer tests and feature ablations, with results across ten seeds.

after.justification: Section 5 and Appendix B report original DMControl experiments, retaining earlier comparisons and adding OPOLO, additional feature variants and stochastic-policy results.

M1.justification: V2 extends the deterministic method with a Gaussian stochastic actor, reparameterized updates and entropy regularization (Appendices B.1 and C.3). Section 4.2 adds autoencoder and adversarial feature objectives. Algorithm 1 also changes from one minibatch to independent batches for witness estimation and policy updating. These are procedural extensions beyond the reformulation of the retained deterministic core.

E1.justification: Both versions evaluate the same ten tasks across the cheetah, walker and quadruped domains of DMControl. The additional baselines, feature variants and stochastic policies use this retained coverage; no new dataset, domain or environmental test scenario is evaluated.

E2.justification: V2 adds OPOLO to the main comparison in Figures 1–3 and Table 1. BC, IQ-Learn, state-only MM and GAIfO remain. The separate TD3 comparison retains MM and GAIfO, so the external comparator expansion is limited to one method.

E3.justification: The new stochastic-policy comparison introduces an entropy-regularized Gaussian-policy configuration with reparameterized action sampling. The retained experiments keep one fixed demonstration, 1M training steps, 1000-step episode truncation, return normalization and the common hyperparameters. Newly documented TD3 architecture settings do not establish that its earlier experiments changed.

E4.justification: V1 compares four feature choices and tests TD3 versus TD7. V2 expands the feature ablation with autoencoder and adversarial representations, testing reconstruction and adversarial feature learning as alternatives to dynamics features. Appendix B.1 additionally tests stochastic versus deterministic policy optimization. The original TD3 robustness analysis is retained, not newly introduced.

E5.justification: Both versions report ten seeds and 95% confidence intervals, including bootstrap intervals for aggregate metrics. V2 additionally reports explicit per-task means and standard deviations in Tables 1–4. This expands uncertainty reporting without establishing an increase in runs or a new significance-testing procedure.

E6.justification: V2 adds OPOLO, autoencoder, adversarial-feature and stochastic-SFM outcomes across the retained tasks, plus aggregate feature-ablation metrics. For example, Table 1 reports OPOLO at 913.6 ± 2.5 on Walker Flip versus SFM at 856.9 ± 64.5. Table 4 adds evidence that stochastic SFM works but trails deterministic variants on some tasks. These are new comparisons, not across-version performance gains; the original TD3 plots are retained.

T1.justification: Section 4 introduces an explicit closed-form reward witness. Propositions 1–2 and Appendix A extend the analysis to stochastic policies and replace the earlier MSE-gradient derivation with witness-weighted policy gradients. V1's standalone Proposition 3 proof and convergence discussion are removed, while the witness formulation retains the feature-gap relationship. Appendix C.3 adds reparameterization and independent-sampling arguments, although Eq. 37 uses the opposite witness sign from Algorithm 1.

C1.justification: The headline contributions remain non-adversarial, state-only imitation from a single demonstration using learned successor features and direct policy optimization. The introduction retains the claimed 16% mean normalized-return advantage and compatibility with off-the-shelf RL algorithms. The added evidence does not redefine these central claims.

C2.justification: V2 explains SFM through a worst-case reward witness and removes the deterministic-solver limitation. It also removes v1's contradictory state-only-feature limitation; state-action features were already permitted in v1 Section 4.1. New interpretations attribute OPOLO's quadruped weakness to inverse-dynamics difficulties and FDM's aggregate advantage over AE/Adv to exploiting dynamics. The exploration limitation remains.

D1.justification: Appendix C adds dedicated TD3 and stochastic implementation sections, network pseudocode, target updates with Polyak factor 0.995, Gaussian parameterization and sampling instructions. The TD3 material documents a previously evaluated variant; the stochastic material supports the new extension. Existing TD7 details, shared hyperparameters, code-access information and hardware/runtime statements are largely retained.

R1.justification: Related work adds R2I and elaborates the previously cited OPOLO approach. New references support stochastic policy gradients, reparameterization and related representation-learning connections; the Agarwal et al. 2022 reference accompanying the removed convergence discussion disappears. The central positioning against adversarial IRL and IQ-Learn remains.

P1.justification: Sections 3–4 are substantially rewritten around consistent probabilistic notation and the witness-based explanation. Limitations move into Discussion, and the appendices are reorganized into proofs, extended results, solver-specific implementation details and hyperparameters. This changes the explanatory narrative and organization beyond adding scientific content.

P2.justification: V2 adds four result tables, an aggregate feature-ablation plot, a stochastic-policy plot and two solver pseudocode blocks. Main comparison plots incorporate OPOLO. V1 Figures 5–6 become appendix Figures 6–7, with the feature plot extended by AE/Adv. The original hyperparameter table is retained as Table 5. These constitute substantial display additions and relocation.

improvement.justification: V2 addresses v1's explicit deterministic-policy limitation with a stochastic formulation, implementation and experiments. OPOLO and the AE/adversarial controls substantially strengthen comparison and analysis of feature choices, while numerical tables and solver-specific details improve assessability and reproducibility. The new appendix has mathematical inconsistencies, notably the opposing witness signs in Algorithm 1 and Eq. 37, so its precision remains imperfect. Nevertheless, the supported extension and stronger empirical scrutiny provide a substantial net improvement.
